parsed.explanation: Under the combined regime, lack of trans recognition and criminalisation of same-sex conduct make birth-sex document reading operative: a trans woman with male-marker documents, or partner relationships authorities read as male-male, can fall within Article 135. If outed, documented severe consequences include interrogation, torture, psychiatric confinement, prison violence and state impunity. No protective border, care, custody, anti-discrimination or remedy is documented; absent traveler-facing incident frequency in a closed media environment is not safety. Minor exposure is unknown but follows the same logic.

entry_documents.exposure: No legal gender recognition; foreign documents mismatching presentation may be read by birth sex, creating criminal exposure under Article 135 if authorities infer male status or same-sex conduct.
entry_documents.protection: Not documented. No border procedure accepting X/diverse markers or protecting mismatched documents is evidenced.
entry_documents.interaction: Document review at borders, hotels, clinics, or police checks can move a traveller from friction into investigation.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Suspects in Article 135 cases face interrogation, torture, confinement to mental hospitals; prison vigilante attacks common; security-service abuses reported with impunity.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: None documented: no anti-discrimination law, no effective complaint or protection for trans travellers.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: If documents reveal male birth sex and presentation causes suspicion, discovery can lead into hostile investigation/custody.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: No gender-recognition or marker-change procedure; detention, hospital or facility placement may follow document birth sex, but specific facility practice is not documented.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Mandatory male-marker records could force birth-sex placement, escalating an ordinary stop or medical emergency into exposure.

care_services.exposure: No trans-specific care access findings; health or psychiatric settings may be hostile, with homosexuality treated as mental disorder and involuntary admission possible.
care_services.interaction: Need for hormones, emergency care, or mental-health support could create document/record exposure to criminal or psychiatric systems.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Government says deviation threatens traditions; rejected UN anti-discrimination requests; 2022 code increased scope/severity; arrests and state torture documented; impunity prevalent.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Threat framing makes police, courts, prisons and mental-health institutions likely to treat an outed trans traveller as criminal/deviant subject.

minors_guardians.exposure: No minor-specific rule; a trans minor or accompanying adult could still face birth-sex reading, psychiatric coercion or state/criminal attention if discovered.
minors_guardians.interaction: Guardians, schools, hotels or clinics may report or disclose identity to authorities; family honour violence is documented for women in official attention.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: Vigilante attacks especially common in prison; relatives report LGBTI people tortured; officials commit abuses with impunity. Police appear more likely source of harm than protection.
street_violence_police_response.protection: No functioning independent monitoring or remedy documented; state media and no civil society prevent verification.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Seeking police help after harassment could out the traveller and invite investigation or detention.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Thin traveler-facing data; incident frequency unverifiable. But documented absence of recourse and expanded penal regime leaves uncertainty weighted toward severe consequences.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Unknown entry/screening practice does not reduce severity; open questions are not protections.

anchor_checks.comparison: Similar to 0.15-A in that discovery can produce severe custody, torture and illusory remedies, but this dossier lacks documented routine arrest solely for presentation or passport mismatch and no credible capital threat.
Materially worse than 0.25-A: fines or release after raids are not the baseline; here suspects face torture, mental-hospital confinement, prison vigilante violence and 2022 criminal-code expansion.
Above 0.35-B: brief identity stops and fines are not the likely consequence; if Article 135 is triggered, imprisonment, torture, psychiatric detention and custody abuse are documented or credible.

parsed.synthesis: The operative regime connects document mismatch, birth-sex reading and Article 135 to severe state responses: interrogation, torture, psychiatric confinement, and prison violence. Trans status is unacknowledged, so protection is absent; hostile official framing and impunity make discovery dangerous. Thin traveler-facing enforcement data does not offset documented severity. For adults and minors, the main risk is being pushed into criminal or psychiatric custody after an ordinary check or medical event.
